title: Syllabus
text: This 2-credit course introduces basic concepts and methods for statistical learning, with an emphasis on modern health science applications. Topics include linear regression with regularization, supervised classification, unsupervised clustering, and dimensionality reduction. The target audience is second-year Biostatistics master’s students or early PhD students with interests in statistical learning techniques for health science data. Students will be trained with hands-on materials to understand the methods, implement the algorithms, and interpret results in real applications.

title: Syllabus
text:
Prerequisites
BIOST 2141, 2142, and 3011. Students are expected to have programming experience in R, or in a low-level language such as C, C++, Java, or Fortran. Prerequisites can be met with other relevant coursework or experience with consent from the instructor.

title: Syllabus
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of this course, students will be able to:

Explain the motivation and intuition behind the statistical learning methods covered in class.
Demonstrate basic theory proofs for selected fundamental concepts and methods.
Implement methods on real datasets in health sciences.
Produce an analysis pipeline and interpret the results in a real application.

Homework policy
Three homework assignments — a mix of theory, simulation, and applied data analysis in R. Submissions are electronic via Canvas. Discussion of homework with classmates is allowed, but each student must independently write and implement their own solution. Solutions are graded on both correctness and clarity. Partial credit is given for identifying gaps in an argument when a complete solution cannot be derived.
Late homework: 80% credit if 0–1 days late, 50% credit if 1–2 days, 0% if more than 2 days. Exceptions for sickness or emergency require the instructor be informed in advance.


Final project
By 11/06, students submit a one-page proposal identifying either a dataset to analyze or a methodological paper to review. On 12/04, each student gives a 5-minute presentation summarizing their work. See the project page for details.

title: Final Project
text:
Tips on choosing a project

For applied projects: pick a dataset where at least two methods from the course are plausibly relevant — that gives you something to compare in your talk. Public health data, genomic/single-cell, EHR-derived, or NHANES-style cohorts all work well.
For methodology reviews: pick a paper recent enough to have follow-up work (so you have something to contextualize) but old enough to have settled into the literature. Aim for one core paper and 2–3 related citations.
Scope honestly: 5 minutes is short. Plan your talk as ~3 main slides plus framing — that’s the unit of analysis to plan around, not the project as a whole.

title: Lab Session: Model Averaging
text:
In this lab, we will explore the concepts of model averaging. We’ll use the mtcars dataset to predict miles per gallon (mpg), which is a regression task. We will build an “ensemble” of different models and show how a weighted average of their predictions can outperform any single model.
Every code cell below runs live in your browser via webR — no local R install needed. Edit any cell and re-run it. Packages load once when the page opens; give it a few seconds on first load.











We will create our “ensemble” by training four different types of models to predict mpg. We’ll use 10-fold cross-validation (CV) to get reliable performance estimates (RMSE) for each one.




















Interpretation: The weighted average (weighted by each model’s inverse cross-validated RMSE) typically beats every individual model, including the single best one from the CV comparison — this is the core intuition behind ensembling: uncorrelated errors partially cancel when averaged, so a blend of mediocre-but-different models can outperform any one strong model.








Live-coding demo: fill in four equal weights (0.25 each) and compare the resulting RMSE to the inverse-RMSE-weighted version above. Then try putting almost all the weight on just one model — at what point does “ensembling” stop helping and just become “using your best single model with extra steps”?

title: Lab Session: Trees, Boosting, Bagging, and Random Forests
text:
In this lab, we will explore tree-based methods for classification. We’ll use the Heart dataset, which contains a binary outcome AHD for 303 patients who presented with chest pain. An outcome value of Yes indicates the presence of heart disease based on an angiographic test, while No means no heart disease. There are \(p=13\) predictors including Age, Sex, Chol (a cholesterol measurement), and other heart and lung function measurements.
Every code cell below runs live in your browser via webR — no local R install needed. Edit any cell and re-run it. Packages load once when the page opens; give it a few seconds on first load. The boosting cell fits 1000 trees and is the slowest cell in this lab.





















We need to evaluate model performance on unseen data. We’ll split the data into a training set (4/5) and a test set (1/5).





































Interpretation: Compare the two confusion matrices above — pruning trades a small amount of training fit for a simpler, more interpretable tree. Whether it costs test accuracy is exactly what these two matrices let you check directly.




Bagging is a random forest where mtry equals the total number of predictors — every tree in the ensemble considers all predictors at each split, so the only randomness comes from bootstrap resampling the training rows.
























Unlike bagging, a genuine random forest restricts each split to a random subset of predictors (mtry = \(\sqrt{p}\) by convention for classification), which decorrelates the trees in the ensemble.








Live-coding demo: fill in mtry with sqrt(ncol(heart) - 1) (the random forest default) first, then re-run with ncol(heart) - 1 (equivalent to bagging) — compare accuracy and the importance rankings between the two.
Try it live: across all four models above (single tree, bagged, boosted, random forest), which has the highest test accuracy? Which is easiest to explain to a non-technical audience? These often aren’t the same model.

title: Lab Session: PCA and PCR
text:
In this lab, we will explore Principal Component Analysis (PCA) as an unsupervised technique for dimensionality reduction and visualization, and then apply Principal Component Regression (PCR) as a supervised learning method. We’ll use the Hitters dataset from the ISLR2 package, which contains statistics for baseball players along with their salaries.
Every code cell below runs live in your browser via webR — no local R install needed. Edit any cell and re-run it. Packages load once when the page opens; give it a few seconds on first load.



First, we load the Hitters dataset. It contains player statistics from the 1986 season and salary data for the 1987 season.










The Salary variable has missing values. We need to remove these observations before proceeding with PCA and PCR, as these methods typically require complete data.











PCA is sensitive to the scale of the variables. Variables with larger variances will disproportionately influence the principal components. Since the predictors in Hitters are on different scales (e.g., number of hits vs. number of years), it’s crucial to standardize them before performing PCA. We use the built-in scaling options in the prcomp and pcr functions rather than scaling manually.



For PCR, we need to evaluate model performance on unseen data. We’ll split the data into a training set (2/3) and a test set (1/3).















PCA is an unsupervised method used to find linear combinations of the original predictors (principal components) that capture the maximum variance in the data. We perform PCA on the predictor variables of the training data. Note that Salary (the response) and non-numeric predictors are excluded from the PCA itself.








Interpretation of PCA Results:

The summary output shows the standard deviation, proportion of variance explained (PVE), and cumulative proportion of variance for each principal component.
The rotation matrix contains the principal component loading vectors. Each column represents a component, and the values are the weights applied to the original scaled variables to create that component.
PC1: The loadings are predominantly positive and largest for career statistics (CAtBat, CHits, CHmRun, CRuns, CRBI, CWalks) and Years. It also gives substantial positive weight to current season offensive stats (AtBat, Hits, Runs, RBI, Walks). This suggests PC1 is a measure of overall career offensive performance and experience.
PC2: Shows a contrast — strong positive loadings for current season offensive performance (AtBat, Hits, Runs, RBI) but negative loadings for Years and career statistics. This component captures current season performance relative to career length. A player scoring high on PC2 might be having a strong current season but is earlier in their career or less accomplished overall than someone with a similar PC1 score.




We can visualize the PVE to help decide how many components capture most of the data’s variability. The scree plot is a common tool for this.













Principal Component Regression (PCR) involves performing regression using the first M principal components as predictors. We use cross-validation to choose the optimal number of components, M, via the pcr function from the pls package.
























Live-coding demo: fill in best_m with the CV-optimal value from the plot above, then try a couple of neighboring values — the test MSE is often fairly flat near the optimum, which is itself a useful lesson about how much precision the CV choice of M actually buys you.

title: Lab Session: Unsupervised Learning — Clustering
text:
In this lab, we will explore two common unsupervised clustering methods: Hierarchical Clustering and K-Means. Our goal is to discover natural groupings within a dataset of European countries based on their employment percentages in different industries.
Every code cell below runs live in your browser via webR — no local R install needed. Edit any cell and re-run it. Packages load once when the page opens; give it a few seconds on first load.



First, we’ll load the Eurojobs dataset. This dataset contains the percentage of the workforce employed in nine different industries for 26 European countries in 1979. It contains 10 variables:

Country: the name of the country (identifier)
Agr: % of workforce employed in agriculture
Min: % in mining
Man: % in manufacturing
PS: % in power supplies industries
Con: % in construction
SI: % in service industries
Fin: % in finance
SPS: % in social and personal services
TC: % in transportation and communications

We will perform some basic exploratory data analysis (EDA) and then — most importantly — scale the data. Scaling is crucial for distance-based algorithms like K-Means and Hierarchical Clustering, as it ensures that variables with larger ranges (e.g., Agriculture) don’t dominate the clustering process over variables with smaller ranges (e.g., Mining).








Now, we scale the data using scale(), which standardizes each column to have a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1.












Hierarchical (or agglomerative) clustering builds a “bottom-up” hierarchy of clusters. It starts with each observation as its own cluster and progressively merges the closest pairs of clusters until all observations are in a single cluster.
We will:

Calculate a distance matrix for our scaled data.
Run the hierarchical clustering algorithm (using “complete” linkage).
Plot the resulting dendrogram to visualize the cluster hierarchy.

















Looking at the dendrogram, we can decide where to “cut” the tree to form clusters. For example, a cut at a height of ~5.0 would give us 4 distinct clusters. We can get the cluster assignments for each country using the cutree() function.








Live-coding demo: fill in k_hc to try different numbers of clusters and see how the country groupings change — a low k lumps very different economies together; a high k starts splitting apart countries that are genuinely similar.




K-Means clustering is a “top-down” approach where we must specify the number of clusters, k, in advance. The algorithm then partitions the data into k clusters, minimizing the within-cluster sum of squares.
The main challenge is choosing the right k. We use two methods to find the optimal k:

Silhouette Method: Measures how similar an observation is to its own cluster compared to other clusters. We look for the k with the highest average silhouette score.
Gap Statistic: Compares the WSS of our data to the WSS of randomly generated “null” reference datasets. We pick the k that maximizes this “gap.”

















Now, let’s run our final K-Means algorithm using the gap statistic’s suggested k.








We can inspect which countries were assigned to which cluster.








Try it live: change centers = best_k_gap to a fixed number like 3 or 5 and re-run — compare the resulting country groupings to what the gap statistic recommended, and to the hierarchical clustering result above.

title: Class 3/Lab1: Subset Selection and Shrinkage
text:
In this lab, we will:

Fit a simple linear regression baseline and interpret its coefficients and prediction intervals.
Compare best subset, forward stepwise, and backward stepwise selection on the insurance dataset.
Fit ridge and lasso regression, and visualize how their coefficient paths differ as the penalty grows.

Every code cell below runs live in your browser via webR — no local R install needed. Edit any cell and re-run it. Packages and data load once when the page opens; give it a few seconds on first load.



Before comparing selection methods, it’s worth fitting the simplest possible model: one predictor, ordinary least squares. We’ll use the neonatal_brain_volumes dataset to relate gestational age (GA) to brain volume.
































Interpretation: The confidence interval describes uncertainty about the mean brain volume at a given gestational age; the (wider) prediction interval describes uncertainty about a single new observation. Every method below is, at its core, still fitting a linear model like this one — just with a strategy for choosing which predictors belong in it.




With more than a couple of predictors, we need a systematic way to choose which ones to include. We’ll compare three approaches on the insurance dataset (predicting charges from the other columns).


























Each row is a model size; each * marks a predictor included at that size.








Live-coding demo: for a small predictor set like this one, the three methods often agree, but that’s not guaranteed in general (forward and backward selection are greedy and can miss the best subset that exhaustive search would find).



regsubsets reports RSS, adjusted \(R^2\), and Mallows’ \(C_p\) for every model size; we compute BIC ourselves from the selected variables at each step.
















Interpretation: RSS and (in-sample) \(R^2\) always improve as you add predictors, so they can’t be used to choose a model size — that’s exactly why \(C_p\), BIC, and adjusted \(R^2\) exist: each penalizes complexity differently, and BIC penalizes it most heavily. Where the red dots land at different sizes across panels is itself the lesson: the “best” model size depends on which tradeoff between fit and parsimony you care about.





Subset selection chooses a hard in/out for each predictor. Ridge and lasso instead shrink coefficients continuously, trading a little bias for a lot less variance. We’ll fit both on the same insurance data, using age and bmi as predictors of charges.


















As \(\lambda\) grows, ridge coefficients shrink smoothly toward zero but rarely hit it exactly; lasso coefficients can be driven to exactly zero, which is what makes it useful for variable selection.



























Interpretation: Cross-validation picks the \(\lambda\) that minimizes out-of-sample error, marked by the left dashed line in each plot (lambda.min); the right dashed line (lambda.1se) gives the most parsimonious model within one standard error of the minimum — a common choice when you’d rather have a simpler model at a small cost in accuracy. Note that with only two predictors, lasso may not zero anything out here; its selection behavior becomes more visible as the predictor set grows.











Interpretation: Ridge and lasso estimates sit closer to the origin than the unpenalized OLS estimate — both are trading a small amount of bias for reduced variance. The shape of the constraint region each method implicitly enforces (a circle for ridge, a diamond for lasso) is what makes lasso capable of setting coefficients to exactly zero, since the diamond’s corners lie on the axes.

Fit ridge and lasso regression, and visualize how their coefficient paths differ as the penalty grows.

Every code cell below runs live in your browser via webR — no local R install needed. Edit any cell and re-run it. Packages and data load once when the page opens; give it a few seconds on first load.



Before comparing selection methods, it’s worth fitting the simplest possible model: one predictor, ordinary least squares. We’ll use the neonatal_brain_volumes dataset to relate gestational age (GA) to brain volume.
































Interpretation: The confidence interval describes uncertainty about the mean brain volume at a given gestational age; the (wider) prediction interval describes uncertainty about a single new observation. Every method below is, at its core, still fitting a linear model like this one — just with a strategy for choosing which predictors belong in it.




With more than a couple of predictors, we need a systematic way to choose which ones to include. We’ll compare three approaches on the insurance dataset (predicting charges from the other columns).


























Each row is a model size; each * marks a predictor included at that size.








Live-coding demo: for a small predictor set like this one, the three methods often agree, but that’s not guaranteed in general (forward and backward selection are greedy and can miss the best subset that exhaustive search would find).



regsubsets reports RSS, adjusted \(R^2\), and Mallows’ \(C_p\) for every model size; we compute BIC ourselves from the selected variables at each step.
















Interpretation: RSS and (in-sample) \(R^2\) always improve as you add predictors, so they can’t be used to choose a model size — that’s exactly why \(C_p\), BIC, and adjusted \(R^2\) exist: each penalizes complexity differently, and BIC penalizes it most heavily. Where the red dots land at different sizes across panels is itself the lesson: the “best” model size depends on which tradeoff between fit and parsimony you care about.





Subset selection chooses a hard in/out for each predictor. Ridge and lasso instead shrink coefficients continuously, trading a little bias for a lot less variance. We’ll fit both on the same insurance data, using age and bmi as predictors of charges.


















As \(\lambda\) grows, ridge coefficients shrink smoothly toward zero but rarely hit it exactly; lasso coefficients can be driven to exactly zero, which is what makes it useful for variable selection.



























Interpretation: Cross-validation picks the \(\lambda\) that minimizes out-of-sample error, marked by the left dashed line in each plot (lambda.min); the right dashed line (lambda.1se) gives the most parsimonious model within one standard error of the minimum — a common choice when you’d rather have a simpler model at a small cost in accuracy. Note that with only two predictors, lasso may not zero anything out here; its selection behavior becomes more visible as the predictor set grows.











Interpretation: Ridge and lasso estimates sit closer to the origin than the unpenalized OLS estimate — both are trading a small amount of bias for reduced variance. The shape of the constraint region each method implicitly enforces (a circle for ridge, a diamond for lasso) is what makes lasso capable of setting coefficients to exactly zero, since the diamond’s corners lie on the axes.

title: Class 2/Lab1: Training, Evaluating, and Resampling Models
text:
In this lab, we will build the toolkit for training and evaluating statistical learning models. Every code cell below runs live in your browser via webR — no local R install needed. Edit any cell and re-run it to see what changes.
Packages load once when the page opens (see the webr: packages: list in the YAML front matter above) — give it a few seconds on first load.
Using simulated data, we will:

Calculate common performance metrics (RMSE, Accuracy, Silhouette Score, Explained Variance) by hand, so the formulas behind caret/yardstick output stop being a black box.
Fit polynomials of increasing degree to the same data and watch training error keep falling while test error eventually turns back up — the bias-variance tradeoff.
Use the bootstrap to estimate the standard error and a confidence interval for a statistic without relying on a textbook formula.




RMSE measures the average magnitude of the errors between predicted and actual values.
\[RMSE = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(predicted_i - actual_i)^2}\]
























Try it live: change set.seed(42) to a different number and re-run all three cells above — watch RMSE change.




Accuracy is the proportion of correct predictions among all cases evaluated — the most common classification metric, though it can be misleading on imbalanced data.
\[Accuracy = \frac{True\,Positives + True\,Negatives}{Total\,Samples}\]
























Live-coding demo: the blank marks the one piece of the accuracy formula left to fill in — true negatives, added alongside true positives in the numerator.




The silhouette score measures how similar a point is to its own cluster (cohesion) versus the nearest other cluster (separation). It ranges from -1 to +1; higher is better.
\[s(i) = \frac{b(i) - a(i)}{\max(a(i), b(i))}\]
where \(a(i)\) is the average distance from point \(i\) to other points in its own cluster, and \(b(i)\) is the average distance from \(i\) to points in the nearest neighboring cluster.
















Try it live: change centers = 2 to centers = 3 or 4 in the first cell and re-run both cells — watch the average silhouette score change as the clustering gets forced into the wrong number of groups.




In PCA, explained variance is the proportion of total variance captured by each principal component — used to decide how many components to keep.
























Try it live: change cov_matrix <- matrix(c(5, 4, 4, 5), nrow = 2) to matrix(c(5, 0, 0, 5), nrow = 2) (zero covariance) and re-run all three cells — watch the first component’s explained variance drop from dominant to about 50%, since the features are no longer correlated.




Here we generate data from a known nonlinear function, then fit polynomials of increasing degree and track training vs. test error. Low-degree models underfit (high bias); high-degree models overfit (high variance).
















Live-coding demo: fill in the blank with a low degree (e.g. 1) — model underfits. Re-run with a high degree (e.g. 10) — model overfits. This #| exercise: blank is the code-blanks pattern: everything else is given, only the one concept-defining value is left for the class to fill in live.








Interpretation: Training error decreases (almost) monotonically as we add flexibility — the model can always fit the training points more closely. Test error decreases at first as bias drops, then rises again once the model starts fitting noise instead of signal. The degree at which test error is minimized is the sweet spot in the bias-variance tradeoff for this dataset.




The bootstrap estimates the sampling distribution of a statistic by resampling the observed data with replacement, without relying on a closed-form formula for its standard error.
























Interpretation: The bootstrap SE and CI closely match what the Central Limit Theorem predicts for the mean of a normal sample (\(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\)), which is why the bootstrap is trustworthy here — and why it’s most useful for statistics (medians, correlations, model coefficients) where no such closed-form formula exists.
Try it live: change statistic_fn <- mean to statistic_fn <- sd or statistic_fn <- median and re-run both cells — the whole pipeline updates. The standard deviation’s bootstrap distribution is noticeably right-skewed in small samples, unlike the mean’s.

title: Class 5/Lab 1: Wine Quality Classification
text:
The objective of this analysis is to classify the quality of red wine into three categories — Low, Medium, and High — based on its physical/chemical properties.
Major steps:

Preprocessing and exploring the wine quality dataset.
Using LASSO regression for feature selection to identify the most important predictors.
Training and comparing three classification models: Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA), Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (QDA), and k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN).
Evaluating model performance on a held-out test set to determine the most effective classifier.

Every code cell below runs live in your browser via webR — no local R install needed. Edit any cell and re-run it. Packages and data load once when the page opens; give it a few seconds on first load. The k-NN cross-validation step near the end is the heaviest computation in this lab and may take a little longer to run.

title: Class 5/Lab 1: Wine Quality Classification
text:
2. Data Preparation & Exploration

Loading Data and Libraries










Creating Quality Classes
The original quality variable is a numeric score from 3 to 8. To frame this as a classification problem, we convert it into a factor with three distinct levels:

Low: Quality score between 0 and 5.
Medium: Quality score of 6.
High: Quality score between 7 and 10.











Distribution of Wine Quality
A bar plot of our new quality_factor variable reveals a significant class imbalance. The Low class is the most prevalent, while the High quality class is relatively rare. This imbalance can make it challenging for models to learn to correctly identify the minority classes.

title: Class 5/Lab 1: Wine Quality Classification
text:
3. Feature Selection with LASSO
With 11 potential predictors, we can use LASSO (L1 Regularization) to automatically select the most influential variables. LASSO penalizes the magnitude of coefficients, shrinking some to exactly zero, which effectively removes them from the model. We use cross-validation to find the optimal regularization strength (lambda).
But first we must create our training and testing samples.

















Lambda vs. Deviance
The plot below shows the cross-validated deviance (a measure of error) for different values of lambda. The dashed vertical line indicates lambda.min, the value that resulted in the lowest deviance.










Selected Variables
Using the optimal lambda, we inspect the model coefficients. Variables with non-zero coefficients are considered important. We can see how each variable influences the prediction for each class.










Interpreting our LASSO results: Key Predictors by Wine Quality

High-Quality Wine: The strongest predictors are low levels of chlorides (large negative coefficient of ~-7.0) and low volatile acidity (~-2.5). This means wines with less chloride and volatile acidity are much more likely to be classified as high quality. Higher levels of sulphates (~+2.0) are also a strong positive predictor for high-quality wine.
Low-Quality Wine: The key indicators for low-quality wine are high levels of volatile acidity (~+3.5) and chlorides (~+3.0). These have the largest positive coefficients. Conversely, lower levels of sulphates (~-1.5) are associated with low-quality wine.
Medium-Quality Wine: This class is less defined by strong predictors. The only notable feature is citric acid (~+1.0), where a higher level is slightly indicative of a medium-quality wine. Most other variables have coefficients near zero, suggesting they don’t help distinguish this class from the others.

Based on a threshold of abs(value) > 0.1, the following variables were selected for subsequent modeling:








Live-coding demo: a lower threshold keeps more variables (less aggressive filtering); a higher threshold keeps only the strongest predictors. This blank is a live version of the modeling choice made in the original analysis (0.1).

title: Class 5/Lab 1: Wine Quality Classification
text:
4. Model Training & Comparison
We now train three classification models using only the subset of features identified by LASSO. We evaluate each model on the held-out test set (25% of the data).

Model 1: Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA)
LDA is a classic classifier that finds linear combinations of predictors to separate the classes.










Model 2: Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (QDA)
QDA is a more flexible version of LDA that allows for quadratic decision boundaries.








Note: QDA’s added flexibility can lead to overfitting relative to LDA, especially with limited training data per class.


Model 3: k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN)
k-NN is a non-parametric method that classifies a data point based on the majority class of its ‘k’ nearest neighbors. We use 10-fold cross-validation to find the optimal value for k. This is the heaviest cell in the lab — give it a moment.

title: Class 5/Lab 1: Wine Quality Classification
text:
5. Conclusion
LDA and k-NN tend to be the most effective models for this classification task, with similar performance. Compare the accuracy and Kappa statistic across all three confusion matrices above — Kappa corrects for chance agreement, so it’s a better tiebreaker than raw accuracy when classes are imbalanced.
Try it live: change the LASSO threshold in the exercise cell above, re-run everything downstream, and see whether a different set of selected variables changes which model wins.

title: Class 6/Lab1: Classification with Support Vector Machines (SVMs)
text:
In this lab, we will:

Load and explore the iris dataset.
Visualize the data to understand the relationships between variables.
Split the data into training and testing sets.
Train three different types of SVM models: linear, polynomial, and radial basis function (RBF).
Evaluate and compare the performance of these models on the test data.

Every code cell below runs live in your browser via webR — no local R install needed. Edit any cell and re-run it. Packages load once when the page opens; give it a few seconds on first load. The polynomial SVM tuning cell fits over 100 models via cross-validation and is the slowest cell in this lab — expect a real wait in-browser.



The iris dataset is a classic dataset in machine learning and is built into R. It contains measurements for 150 iris flowers from three different species: setosa, versicolor, and virginica.








Interpretation of the Data: The dataset has 150 observations and 5 variables. Sepal.Length, Sepal.Width, Petal.Length, and Petal.Width are all numeric, and Species is a categorical variable with 3 levels. There are 50 samples for each of the three species.




Visualizing the data is a crucial step to understand the separability of the classes. We create two scatter plots: one for sepal dimensions and one for petal dimensions. We color the points by Species to see how distinct the groups are.








Plot Interpretation: The species are much more clearly separated when we plot them by their petal dimensions. The sepal dimensions show significant overlap, especially between the versicolor and virginica species. For this lab, we will intentionally use the more challenging sepal features to see how well SVM can perform.




To evaluate our model’s performance on unseen data, we must split our dataset into a training set (used to build the model) and a testing set (used to evaluate it). We’ll use an 80/20 split.
We use the createDataPartition function from the caret package to create a stratified split, which ensures that the proportion of each species is the same in both the training and testing sets.
Note: For this analysis, we are only using Sepal.Length and Sepal.Width as our predictors.












Now we’ll train three SVM models with different kernels using train() from caret, which automates hyperparameter tuning via cross-validation.




























After training, we evaluate each model on the held-out test set. A confusion matrix shows exactly where each model made correct and incorrect predictions per class.
































Interpretation: Compare accuracy and per-class sensitivity across the three confusion matrices above. All three kernels tend to identify setosa perfectly (it’s linearly separable even on the harder sepal features), but differ on how well they separate versicolor from virginica, which overlap more. If the RBF kernel comes out ahead, that suggests the true decision boundary between those two species is non-linear.





This exercise demonstrates the importance of testing different kernels and tuning hyperparameters to find the best model for a given dataset — the “best” kernel isn’t knowable in advance, only by comparing held-out performance.
Try it live: re-run the training-and-testing split cell with a different set.seed() value, then re-run all three SVM cells — see whether the same kernel wins on a different train/test split.
